items.prompt: Which hiragana represents the vowel /i/ in the five-vowel card?
items.example: あ　い　う　え　お

choices.rationale: Correct. い is the Japanese vowel /i/.
え represents /e/, not /i/.
あ represents /a/, not /i/.

items.explanation: The order is あ /a/, い /i/, う /u/, え /e/, お /o/. The slashes name sound categories, not English letter names.

items.prompt: Which kana is the Japanese vowel /u/?
items.example: あ　い　う　え　お

choices.rationale: Correct. う represents /u/, generally produced with little lip rounding.
お represents /o/, which is a different vowel.
い represents /i/.

items.explanation: う represents Japanese /u/. Its articulation is typically less lip-rounded than the English vowel in “food.”

items.prompt: Which vowel card corresponds to /e/, rather than /a/ or /o/?
items.example: あ　い　う　え　お

choices.rationale: Correct. え corresponds to /e/.
あ is /a/, a more open vowel.
お is /o/, made farther back in the mouth.

items.explanation: え is /e/, a relatively steady vowel. Avoid turning it into an English-style two-part glide.

items.prompt: How many regular timing units (morae) are in いえ (house)?

choices.rationale: Correct. Each kana here corresponds to one mora.
Japanese いえ has two distinct vowel units, not one English-style glide.
There is no extra え in the written example.

items.explanation: いえ is い・え, two morae. You can mark two evenly spaced taps while reading the written card.

items.prompt: Which breakdown shows the three morae of あおい (blue)?

choices.rationale: Correct. Each of the three vowel kana is a separate mora.
あ and お are separate vowel morae, not one merged English diphthong.

choices.text: あおい as a single beat
choices.rationale: The written word has three morae, even if a beginner says it quickly.

items.explanation: あおい contains three separate vowel morae: あ /a/, お /o/, い /i/. The word means “blue” as an adjective.

items.prompt: In the timing exercise, how does ああ differ from あ?

choices.text: ああ takes two morae; あ takes one.
choices.rationale: Correct. The extra vowel is an extra timing unit.

choices.text: Both always take exactly one mora.
choices.rationale: A repeated vowel adds another timing unit in this written exercise.

choices.text: ああ adds a consonant sound.
choices.rationale: Both characters are vowels; no consonant is added.

items.explanation: The visual contrast previews vowel length. It is a timing exercise, not a claim that both spellings have the same meaning.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes Japanese う compared with English “oo” in “food”?

choices.text: It is usually made with less lip rounding; the English comparison is only a rough guide.
choices.rationale: Correct. Japanese /u/ is commonly unrounded or compressed, not identical to English /uː/.

choices.text: They are always exactly the same sound.
choices.rationale: Japanese /u/ differs in typical lip posture and can vary by speaker and context.
う is a vowel kana and can represent a pronounced mora.

items.explanation: English vowel labels are only temporary hints. Listen to authentic Japanese later to learn the actual sound, especially the lip posture of /u/.
